content: The outcomes of interest were assessed over a follow-up period of up to 32 years. Influence analyses were performed for each outcome by systematically removing one study at a time to evaluate the individual effect of each study on the pooled results. This approach was used to determine whether any single study disproportionately influenced the overall findings. No single study was found to significantly alter the magnitude or direction of the pooled results. Baseline dietary intake was assessed differently across the included studies, typically using methods such as food frequency questionnaires, diet records, or 24-hour dietary recalls conducted at least once at baseline. While these self-reported methods may introduce variability in exposure assessment, many of the dietary assessment tools used had been validated. The differences in dietary assessment methods across studies were not considered a significant source of bias. The heterogeneity among studies, as indicated by an I² value greater than 50%, was significant and could not be fully explained by sensitivity, subgroup, or meta-regression analyses where these were conducted. This led to a downgrading of the evidence by one level. For observational studies, the observed heterogeneity may have been due to statistical rather than clinical differences, but a conservative approach was taken by downgrading the evidence. For randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the outcome included all types of strokes, whereas for observational studies, the outcome was limited to ischemic stroke. The 95% confidence interval (CI) crossed a threshold of important benefit or harm, leading to a downgrading of the evidence by one level. Of the 177 data points used in the multiple regression analysis, 113 represented saturated fatty acid (SFA) intakes of less than 10% of total energy intake, and 65 represented intakes of less than 8%. Residual analysis indicated a linear relationship between SFA intake and its effect on blood lipids across the entire range of SFA intakes, including levels above and below 10% of total energy intake. All studies included in the multiple regression analysis of blood lipids were strictly controlled dietary trials lasting between 13 and 91 days, during which protein and cholesterol intakes were held constant. Some parallel-design studies were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias regarding randomization due to insufficient description of the randomization procedure. However, studies with crossover and Latin-square designs were considered to have a low risk of bias for randomization, as all participants were intended to receive all treatments, minimizing the likelihood of systematic baseline differences affecting the results. Blinding was not considered a significant source of bias, as all interventions involved food provision. While participants in some studies may have been able to distinguish between intervention and control diets, this was not expected to affect compliance due to the study design and conduct. Bias from unblinded outcome assessment was assessed as low. There was no evidence of widespread attrition bias or selective reporting, and other sources of bias were minimal. Overall, the studies were judged to have a low risk of bias. The analysis was conducted as a multiple regression in which data points were directly extracted from each study rather than using mean differences between groups within each study. This approach did not allow for direct quantitative measurement of between-study variability. However, qualitative assessment of the included studies and the consistency of the multiple regression results suggested that any inconsistency was likely minor and not serious. Low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, while an indirect measure of patient-important cardiovascular outcomes, is a well-established biomarker for assessing the effects of interventions on cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. It is widely considered a causal factor for atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease. Therefore, the evidence was not downgraded for indirectness. Imprecision was assessed using the 95% CI of the regression coefficient as a proxy for the 95% CI of a pooled estimate of effect. The regression coefficient provided an estimate of the effect of reducing SFA intake on LDL cholesterol, and the 95% CI measured the variability of that effect. The 95% CI did not cross a threshold of irrelevant benefit or important harm. The interventions analyzed were not limited to those modifying SFA intake but also included studies in which other dietary fats were modified. The risk of publication bias was considered low. For RCT outcomes other than LDL cholesterol, the polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) used as replacements for SFA were predominantly of plant origin. For LDL cholesterol outcomes, the PUFAs used were primarily linoleic acid and α-linolenic acid. In observational studies, the PUFAs were mixed. The total number of participants was reported, and the relative effect was interpreted as the change in LDL cholesterol when 1% of total energy intake as SFA was replaced with an isocaloric amount of PUFAs. The absolute effect in real-world settings depends on baseline risk, which can vary across populations. The included RCTs were primarily conducted in populations from Australia, Europe, New Zealand, and the United States, while observational studies included populations from North America, Europe, Asia, Australia, the United Kingdom, and multinational cohorts. Significant differences in physiological responses to SFA intake across different ethnic groups or geographic settings were not anticipated. Most RCTs used appropriate methods for random sequence generation, and about half had good allocation concealment. Blinding was generally not feasible in dietary trials, but no other biases were noted. Compliance with long-term behavioral interventions, such as those used in these studies, can vary widely, potentially attenuating the pooled effect and biasing it toward the null. The 95% CI crossed thresholds of both important benefit and harm in some cases, leading to downgrading of the evidence by two levels. Visual inspection of funnel plots or other assessments did not suggest publication bias. In cases where there were too few studies to conduct funnel plot analysis, it was assumed that the subset of studies did not exhibit publication bias, as no indication of such bias was found in the larger group of studies. Large prospective observational studies included well-balanced populations with no major differences between exposed and unexposed groups. These studies were well-controlled for potential confounders, although residual confounding could not be entirely ruled out. Cohorts were followed for sufficient durations, up to 32 years, to assess outcomes of interest.
